lessonTitle: Towards Personalised Prescribing: Using Genotype to Guide Drug Choice and Dose

blocks.text: Two patients are prescribed the same antiepileptic at the same dose. One has no problems. The other, who carries a particular immune gene variant, develops a blistering skin reaction that can strip the skin and kill. A cheap cheek swab before the first tablet could have separated them. Personalised prescribing aims to make that kind of choice routine, but it also raises questions of cost, certainty and privacy.

blocks.markdown: **Pharmacogenomics** studies how a person's genetic make-up influences their response to drugs. The goal of **personalised (stratified) prescribing** is to use genotype, alongside age, organ function, comorbidity and interacting drugs, to choose the right drug and dose first time. A genotype result can change management in three main ways: **avoid** a drug, **choose** a different drug, or **adjust** the dose.

blocks.title: Pharmacogenetic test
blocks.text: A pharmacogenetic test identifies a germline variant (for example in a drug-metabolising enzyme, transporter, drug target or immune gene) that is associated with a predictable change in drug response or risk of toxicity. Tests may be reactive (ordered when a drug is being considered) or pre-emptive (a panel done in advance and stored for future decisions).

blocks.caption: Examples of how a genotype result may change prescribing.
rows: HLA-B*1502 (relevant in patients of some Asian ancestries)
Greatly increased risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
Test before starting where indicated; if positive, avoid and choose another antiepileptic
Lower dose requirement and higher bleeding risk at standard doses
Genotype-informed starting dose, with INR monitoring (routine benefit debated)
Reduced hepatic uptake, higher plasma levels, increased myopathy risk
Use a lower dose or an alternative statin
Test before treatment; reduce dose or avoid

blocks.title: Interpreting a genotype result
blocks.prompt: A 62-year-old man is to start warfarin. Genotyping shows CYP2C9*1/*3 and a VKORC1 variant associated with increased sensitivity. How might this alter management, and what must still be done?

steps.text: CYP2C9*3 reduces metabolism of the more potent S-warfarin, so clearance is lower and exposure is higher at a given dose.
The VKORC1 variant lowers the amount of the target enzyme or makes it more sensitive, so a lower plasma concentration produces the same anticoagulation.
Both variants imply a lower maintenance dose requirement, so a lower starting dose, or a genotype-guided dosing algorithm, is considered.

Genotype explains only part of the variability in warfarin dose. Age, weight, diet, co-medications, liver function and adherence also matter, so the INR must still be monitored closely and the dose titrated.

blocks.answer: Choose a lower starting dose, but continue regular INR monitoring because genotype is only one determinant.

blocks.markdown: **Limits and costs of routine testing.** A genotype is not a diagnosis: it changes probability, not certainty. Many variants have incomplete penetrance, and non-genetic factors (age, kidney and liver function, interactions, adherence) often explain more variation than genes. Evidence from randomised trials of testing is available for only some gene-drug pairs and results vary, so health systems recommend routine testing only where benefit is clear. Allele frequencies differ by ancestry, so a panel developed in one population may miss relevant variants in another. Costs include the test, turnaround time (a result that arrives after treatment must begin is of little use), interpretation support and system integration.

blocks.caption: p = frequency of the variant in the tested population; r = risk (probability) of the adverse reaction in carriers who are treated. This gives the number of patients who must be tested to prevent one reaction, assuming testing leads carriers to avoid the drug.

blocks.title: Is a test worthwhile? A simple calculation
blocks.prompt: A variant has a frequency of 4% in a population. If treated, 25% of carriers develop a severe reaction. A test costs 60 currency units per patient. Calculate the number needed to genotype to prevent one reaction and the cost of doing so. (Illustrative numbers.)

steps.text: Cost per reaction prevented = 100 patients x 60 = 6000 units, ignoring the savings from the avoided reaction.
Judge the result against the cost and severity of the reaction: if one reaction costs far more than 6000 units in hospital care, or is life-threatening, testing may be worthwhile.

blocks.answer: 100 patients tested, costing 6000 units per reaction prevented before accounting for savings

blocks.title: Predictive value
blocks.text: A test is most useful when the variant is common enough, the risk it carries is high, the reaction is severe and unpredictable by other means, an alternative drug exists, and the result arrives in time to inform the decision.

blocks.markdown: **Ethical issues.** Genetic data are different from most clinical data because they are lifelong, they are shared with biological relatives, and they may reveal more than was asked for. Key issues are **informed consent** (what is tested, who sees the result, how long it is kept), **privacy and confidentiality** (secure storage, limits on access), **familial implications** (a result in one person says something about relatives who have not consented), **incidental or secondary findings** (variants unrelated to the drug question), **discrimination** (insurance, employment) and **equity** (research databases skewed towards some ancestries mean that results are less reliable for others, and testing may be unequally available).

items: Consent should cover purpose, storage duration, sharing, and use in research or future prescribing.
Data should be stored securely in the health record, with access limited to those who need it and compliance with data protection law.
Decide in advance how incidental findings will be handled and whether the patient wishes to be informed.
Counselling should explain that results can have implications for relatives and may be permanent.
Patients retain the right to decline testing without penalty to their care.

blocks.title: Negative does not mean safe
blocks.text: A negative result for one variant does not exclude the adverse reaction, because other genetic and non-genetic causes exist. Continue to monitor and counsel patients as normal.

points: A genotype result can lead to avoiding a drug, choosing an alternative, or adjusting the dose, but it changes risk rather than giving certainty.
Routine testing depends on variant frequency, size of risk, severity of harm, availability of alternatives, timeliness and cost-effectiveness, so it is justified only for some gene-drug pairs.
Genetic data raise ethical questions about consent, privacy, family implications, incidental findings, discrimination and equity.

questions.stem: Genotyping for HLA-B*1502 is advised before carbamazepine in some populations. What risk is it predicting?

options.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
Reduced absorption of carbamazepine
Warfarin resistance
Hepatic enzyme induction

questions.correctOptionText: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the allele is strongly associated with these severe cutaneous reactions.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: the allele is an immune gene, not an absorption factor.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: carbamazepine induces enzymes in everyone, regardless of this allele.

questions.explanation: HLA-B*1502 is an immune-recognition gene variant strongly associated with severe cutaneous hypersensitivity to carbamazepine. A positive result leads to avoidance of the drug and choice of an alternative.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is due to start fluorouracil-based chemotherapy for colorectal cancer. Pre-treatment testing shows a DPYD variant associated with reduced dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Reduce the starting dose, or avoid the drug if activity is absent, and monitor closely for toxicity
Give the standard dose and ignore the result
Increase the dose to compensate for reduced enzyme activity
Add an enzyme inducer to restore enzyme activity

questions.correctOptionText: Reduce the starting dose, or avoid the drug if activity is absent, and monitor closely for toxicity

distractorRationale.a: Correct: reduced DPD activity slows fluorouracil breakdown, so exposure and toxicity risk rise and the dose must be reduced or the drug avoided.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: standard doses risk severe, potentially fatal toxicity.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: raising the dose would worsen toxicity.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: an inducer would not reliably restore the deficient enzyme and is not recommended.

questions.explanation: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase is the main route of fluorouracil breakdown, so reduced activity causes drug accumulation and severe toxicity such as mucositis and neutropenia. Genotype-guided dose reduction, or avoidance when activity is absent, with careful monitoring, lowers the risk.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why a patient with CYP2C9 and VKORC1 variants often needs a lower warfarin dose?

options.text: Reduced warfarin metabolism and increased sensitivity of the target enzyme
Increased warfarin absorption only
Faster renal excretion of warfarin
Reduced plasma protein binding of vitamin K

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced warfarin metabolism and increased sensitivity of the target enzyme

distractorRationale.a: Correct: CYP2C9 variants lower clearance and VKORC1 variants raise sensitivity.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: absorption is not the explanation.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: faster excretion would raise the dose needed.

questions.explanation: Both a pharmacokinetic effect (lower clearance via CYP2C9) and a pharmacodynamic effect (greater target sensitivity via VKORC1) increase anticoagulation at a given dose. Hence lower doses are needed to keep the INR in range.

questions.stem: A pharmacogenetic test costs 50 currency units per patient. The variant frequency in the tested population is 5% (0.05). Calculate the testing cost per carrier identified, in currency units.
questions.explanation: To find one carrier you must test 1 / 0.05 = 20 patients on average, costing 20 x 50 = 1000 units. Rarer variants therefore make screening more expensive per carrier found.

questions.stem: A variant has a frequency of 2% (0.02) in a population. If treated, 40% (0.40) of carriers develop a severe adverse reaction, and testing allows all carriers to avoid the drug. Using number needed to genotype = 1 / (p x r), calculate how many patients must be tested to prevent one reaction.
questions.explanation: p x r = 0.02 x 0.40 = 0.008, so the number needed to genotype is 1 / 0.008 = 125 patients. If a test costs a given amount, multiply it by 125 to obtain the cost per reaction prevented.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a limitation of routine pharmacogenetic testing?

options.text: Genotype explains only part of the variability in drug response, since non-genetic factors also matter
Genotype changes during the patient's life
Genetic tests cannot detect any drug-related variants
A negative result guarantees that no adverse reaction will occur

questions.correctOptionText: Genotype explains only part of the variability in drug response, since non-genetic factors also matter

distractorRationale.a: Correct: age, organ function, interactions and adherence also contribute.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: many clinically useful variants are detectable.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: a negative test does not rule out reactions.

questions.explanation: Response depends on genes and on many non-genetic influences, so a genotype only modifies risk. This is why monitoring and clinical judgement remain necessary after testing.

questions.stem: Discuss the limits and cost considerations of introducing routine pharmacogenetic testing for a new gene-drug pair.
markingGuide: Genotype alters probability but not certainty; incomplete penetrance; non-genetic factors
Evidence of clinical benefit and cost-effectiveness may be limited; randomised data for few pairs
Variant frequency and risk determine number needed to test and cost per event prevented
Allele frequencies vary by ancestry, so panels may miss variants in some populations
Practical costs: test price, turnaround time, interpretation support, IT integration, staff training
Test is most justified when reaction is severe, alternatives exist and the result is available before treatment
questions.explanation: A rational decision weighs the benefit (events prevented, severity) against the cost and practical limits of testing. The balance differs by gene-drug pair and by population.

questions.stem: A patient's pharmacogenetic result unexpectedly shows a variant known to carry a heritable disease risk for relatives. Which ethical issue is most directly raised?

options.text: Incidental findings and the implications of genetic information for relatives
Therapeutic drug monitoring
Bioequivalence of generic drugs
First-pass metabolism

questions.correctOptionText: Incidental findings and the implications of genetic information for relatives

distractorRationale.a: Correct: genetic data are shared with biological relatives and may reveal unrequested information.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: this relates to drug level monitoring.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: this is a pharmacokinetic concept.

questions.explanation: Unlike most clinical data, genetic information bears on relatives who have not consented to testing. Consent should therefore address how incidental findings will be handled and whether the patient wishes to be told.

questions.stem: Discuss the ethical issues involved in storing and using a patient's genetic data in the health record for future prescribing decisions.
markingGuide: Informed consent: purpose, duration of storage, who can access, research use
Privacy and confidentiality: secure storage, access limits and data protection compliance
Familial implications: results concern relatives who have not consented; duty and limits regarding disclosure
Incidental findings: policy and patient preference on being informed
Risk of discrimination (insurance, employment) and stigma
Equity: databases biased to some ancestries, unequal access, and the right to decline testing without affecting care
questions.explanation: Genetic data are permanent, identifying and shared with relatives, so their storage and use need stronger safeguards than most clinical data. Consent and governance should be explicit.

questions.stem: True or false: a negative result for a tested pharmacogenetic variant guarantees that the patient will not experience the associated adverse reaction.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Reactions can arise from other genetic variants and from non-genetic factors, and tests rarely have perfect predictive value. A negative result lowers risk but monitoring and counselling remain necessary.
